skills.title: Observation
skills.summary: An observation is information gathered directly with your senses or instruments, without adding explanation.
objectives: Describe what you directly sense or measure
Tell an observation apart from an opinion

skills.title: Inference
skills.summary: An inference is a conclusion or explanation you reach by reasoning from observations — it goes beyond what you directly sense.
objectives: Distinguish an observation from an inference
Explain the reasoning behind an inference

skills.title: Testable Questions
skills.summary: A testable question can be answered by gathering evidence through observation or experiment.
objectives: Rewrite an untestable question so it can be tested

skills.title: Hypotheses
skills.summary: A hypothesis is a testable, reasoned prediction about what will happen and why.
objectives: State a hypothesis as a testable prediction with a reason
Tell a hypothesis apart from a guess

skills.title: Evidence and Conclusions
skills.summary: Evidence is data that supports or challenges a claim. A conclusion follows from evidence, and correlation does not prove causation.
objectives: Use evidence to support or challenge a claim
Explain why correlation does not always mean causation

components.body: Describe what you directly sense or measure, without adding explanation.
An observation is what you can see, hear, feel, smell, or measure right now. 'The ground is wet' is an observation. Saying 'it rained' is not — that is a guess about the cause.
An observation records information from the senses or an instrument. It does not include why something happened.
Looking at a plant: 'The leaves are yellow' is an observation. 'The plant is sick' is not — that is an explanation you added.
Adding a cause or opinion turns an observation into something else. Keep observations to what you directly detect.
Observation = what you directly sense or measure, with no explanation attached.
Reach a reasoned conclusion from observations and label it as an inference.
An observation is what you directly sense. An inference goes one step further.
If you observe wet ground and puddles, you might infer that it rained. The inference is your explanation — it could be wrong (a sprinkler may have run).
Observation: 'The window is broken and there is a ball inside.' Inference: 'A ball broke the window.' The inference explains the observations but is not something you directly saw.
Inference = a conclusion reasoned from observations; it may be wrong and needs evidence.
Recognize questions that can be answered by gathering evidence.
A testable question can be answered by observing or experimenting. 'Does more water make a plant grow taller?' is testable. 'Are roses the best flower?' is not — it is an opinion.
Turn 'Is music good?' into a testable question: 'Do students score higher on a memory test with music or with silence?'
Testable question = one you can answer with observation or experiment, not opinion.
Write a hypothesis as a testable prediction with a reason.
A hypothesis predicts what will happen and gives a reason. It is more than a guess because it can be tested and explained.
A common form is: 'If [change], then [predicted result], because [reason].'
'If a plant gets more sunlight, then it will grow taller, because sunlight provides energy for growth.' This is testable and gives a reason.
Hypothesis = a testable prediction with a reason, not just a guess.
Use evidence to support a conclusion, and avoid confusing correlation with causation.
Evidence is data that supports or challenges a claim. A conclusion should follow from the evidence — not from what you hoped to find.
Two things that rise and fall together are correlated. Correlation does not prove that one causes the other; a third factor may cause both.
Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. They are correlated, but ice cream does not cause sunburn — hot, sunny weather raises both.
Do not assume that because two things happen together, one causes the other.
Evidence supports conclusions; correlation alone does not prove causation.

hints.text: An observation is something you can directly sense right now.
The other choices explain a cause you did not directly see.

questions.explanation: You can directly see that the ground is wet. The other statements add an explanation, so they are inferences.

hints.text: An inference is a conclusion you reason to, not something you directly see.

questions.explanation: 'It rained recently' is a conclusion reasoned from the observations; the others are the observations themselves.

questions.prompt: How is an inference different from an observation?

options: It adds reasoning that goes beyond what you sense

answer_spec.correct_answer: It adds reasoning that goes beyond what you sense

hints.text: Inferences can be wrong; observations are what you detect.

questions.explanation: An inference reasons beyond the direct observation, so it can be wrong and needs evidence.

options: Does more sunlight make plants grow taller?

hints.text: A testable question can be answered by gathering evidence.

I think the plant will do something

questions.prompt: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. What is the best conclusion?

options: They are correlated, but one may not cause the other
Sunburns cause people to buy ice cream

answer_spec.correct_answer: They are correlated, but one may not cause the other

hints.text: Two things rising together does not prove one causes the other.
Hot, sunny weather could raise both.

questions.explanation: The two are correlated, but a third factor (hot, sunny weather) likely drives both — correlation is not causation.
